title: Magnetism & Electromagnetism
description: Magnets, magnetic fields, electromagnets, the motor effect, electromagnetic induction, generators, and transformers.

notes.heading: Magnets and Magnetic Fields
notes.body: A magnet has two poles: North (N) and South (S). Like poles repel; unlike poles attract. Magnetic materials: iron, cobalt, nickel, and their alloys (steel). NOT all metals are magnetic (aluminium, copper, gold are NOT). A magnetic field is the region around a magnet where magnetic forces act. Field lines: run from North to South outside the magnet (South to North inside — forming closed loops). Closer lines = stronger field. The Earth has a magnetic field — its magnetic south pole is near the geographic North Pole (compass N points to magnetic south). Plotting compasses trace field lines. Iron filings align along field lines when sprinkled around a magnet.

notes.heading: Electromagnets
notes.body: An electromagnet is a solenoid (coil of wire) wrapped around a soft iron core. When current flows, a magnetic field is produced (right-hand grip rule: fingers curl in current direction, thumb = N pole). Electromagnets: can be switched on/off, strength can be varied (increase current, more coil turns, add iron core), polarity can be reversed (reverse current). Uses: scrapyard cranes (lift iron/steel), electric bells, relays, magnetic locks, MRI scanners, circuit breakers, loudspeakers. A permanent magnet always has a magnetic field but cannot be switched off. Comparison: electromagnets are temporary, controllable; permanent magnets are always on, don't need power.

notes.heading: The Motor Effect
notes.body: A current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field experiences a force — the motor effect. Force is maximum when current ⊥ field (90°). Force = 0 when current ∥ field. Fleming's Left-Hand Rule (for motors): ThuMb = Motion (force), First finger = Field (N→S), Second finger = Current (+ → −). Increasing force: stronger magnet, larger current, more wire in field (coil). Electric motor: a coil rotates between magnet poles. Split-ring commutator reverses current every half-turn → coil keeps rotating in same direction. Brushes conduct current to commutator. Energy conversion: electrical → kinetic (+ heat/sound dissipated).

notes.heading: Electromagnetic Induction (Generator Effect)
notes.body: Moving a conductor through a magnetic field (or changing the magnetic field around a conductor) induces a voltage (potential difference). This is electromagnetic induction. If the conductor is part of a complete circuit, an induced current flows. Factors increasing induced voltage: stronger magnet, faster movement, more coil turns. Fleming's Right-Hand Rule (for generators): ThuMb = Motion, First finger = Field, Second finger = Current. Generator: coil rotates in magnetic field → voltage induced. Slip rings + brushes → alternating current (AC). Split-ring commutator → direct current (DC). Energy conversion: kinetic → electrical. This is the principle behind power stations (steam/water/wind turns turbine → spins generator → electricity).

notes.heading: Transformers
notes.body: A transformer changes the voltage of an alternating current (only works with AC — needs changing magnetic field). Two coils wound on a shared iron core: Primary coil (input, Vp, Np turns). Secondary coil (output, Vs, Ns turns). Equation: Vp/Vs = Np/Ns. Step-up transformer: Ns > Np → Vs > Vp (more turns on secondary → higher voltage, lower current). Step-down transformer: Ns < Np → Vs < Vp. Assuming 100% efficiency: input power = output power → Vp×Ip = Vs×Is. If voltage steps up, current steps down proportionally. Why high voltage transmission? P=I²R losses in cables. Transmitting at very high voltage → low current → less energy wasted as heat. National Grid uses step-up transformers (to ~400,000 V for transmission) and step-down transformers (to 230 V for homes).

notes.heading: The National Grid and Power Transmission
notes.body: The National Grid distributes electricity from power stations to consumers. Power stations generate at ~25,000 V. Step-up transformers increase to ~400,000 V for long-distance transmission (reduces current → reduces P=I²R heat losses in cables). Step-down transformers reduce voltage in stages: substations → 11,000 V for local distribution → 230 V for homes. Overhead cables: aluminium (lightweight, good conductor) with steel core (strength). Underground cables: used in cities but more expensive and harder to cool/repair. Advantages of the grid: power can be routed from anywhere to anywhere, supply matches demand, different sources can contribute (renewables and non-renewables work together).

notes.heading: Loudspeakers and Microphones
notes.body: Loudspeaker (motor effect): AC current in coil → alternating force in permanent magnetic field → coil vibrates → attached cone vibrates → sound waves produced. Frequency of AC = frequency of sound. Microphone (generator effect): sound waves → diaphragm vibrates → coil moves in magnetic field → voltage induced → AC signal. This electrical signal can then be amplified and sent to loudspeakers. Loudspeaker = electrical → kinetic → sound. Microphone = sound → kinetic → electrical. Both use the same electromagnetic principles in reverse directions — a lovely symmetry.

flashcards.definition: Region where magnetic forces act. Lines run N→S outside magnet. Closer lines = stronger field.
flashcards.example: Iron filings around a bar magnet trace out the field line pattern.

flashcards.definition: Solenoid (coil) + iron core. Magnetic field when current flows. Can be switched on/off; strength controlled.
flashcards.example: Scrapyard crane — switch on to lift car, switch off to drop.

flashcards.definition: Force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field. Maximum when wire ⊥ field.
flashcards.example: Fleming's Left-Hand Rule: ThuMb=Motion, First finger=Field, Second finger=Current.

flashcards.definition: For MOTORS: Thumb=Force(motion), First=Field, Second=Current. All mutually perpendicular.
Moving a conductor through a magnetic field induces a voltage. Generator effect.
flashcards.example: Bicycle dynamo — magnet spins near coil → voltage induced → lights on.

flashcards.definition: Reverses current direction every half-turn in a DC motor, keeping coil rotating same way.
Maintain continuous connection in AC generator → produces alternating current (current direction reverses).
Vp/Vs = Np/Ns. Step-up: Ns>Np → Vs>Vp. Step-down: Ns<Np → Vs<Vp. AC only.
P=I²R losses. Higher V → lower I for same P → less heat wasted in cables.
flashcards.example: National Grid: 400,000 V transmission → minimal current → minimal power loss.

flashcards.definition: For a solenoid: fingers curl in current direction → thumb points to North pole of electromagnet.
flashcards.example: If current flows counterclockwise (looking from N), the facing end is North.

flashcards.definition: AC in coil → alternating motor effect force → cone vibrates at AC frequency → sound waves.
flashcards.example: Audio signal at 440 Hz → cone vibrates at 440 Hz → musical note A produced.

flashcards.definition: Permanent: always magnetic field, can't switch off. Electro: magnetic only when current flows, controllable strength.
flashcards.example: Fridge door uses permanent magnet. Scrapyard crane uses electromagnet.

questions.stem: Two N poles facing each other:
questions.explanation: Like poles repel each other. Only unlike poles (N-S) attract.

choices: Increase current, turns, or add iron core
questions.explanation: More current = stronger field. More turns = stronger field. Iron core concentrates field lines.

questions.stem: Main advantage of electromagnet over permanent?
choices: Can be switched on/off and strength varied
questions.explanation: Controllability is the key advantage. Switching off current → magnetism disappears.
Motor: electrical energy from power supply → kinetic energy of rotating shaft (some wasted as heat in coils).

questions.stem: Field lines outside bar magnet run:
questions.explanation: Outside: N→S. Inside magnet: S→N (forming closed loops).

questions.stem: Why must transformers use AC, not DC?
choices: Changing magnetic field is needed to induce voltage in secondary — DC produces constant field, no induction
DC would melt the iron core
questions.explanation: Electromagnetic induction requires a CHANGING magnetic field. AC provides continuously changing field. DC = steady field → no induced voltage.

choices: Fleming's Right-Hand Rule — motion + field → current (generator)
questions.explanation: Right hand = Generator (induction). Left hand = Motor (force). Both use thumb=motion, first=field, second=current.

choices: Reverses current every half-turn so coil keeps rotating same direction
questions.explanation: Without commutator, coil would stop after 90° (forces balance). Commutator swaps connections → current reverses → torque continues same direction.

questions.stem: Why transmit electricity at very high voltage?
choices: Reduces current → reduces P=I²R heat losses in transmission cables
questions.explanation: For same power (P=VI), higher V means lower I. Lower I means less energy wasted heating the cables (P_waste=I²R).
Sound vibrates diaphragm → coil moves in magnetic field → voltage induced → electrical signal. Generator effect in reverse of loudspeaker.

questions.stem: Right-hand grip rule: fingers curl in ___ direction, thumb points to ___ of electromagnet.
questions.explanation: Grip the solenoid with right hand: fingers follow conventional current direction around coil; thumb extends to N pole.

questions.stem: Step-up transformer: Ns=2000, Np=200, Vp=25V. Vs=?
questions.explanation: Vs=25×(2000/200)=25×10=250 V. Step-up: output voltage > input.

questions.stem: Slip rings in AC generator vs split-ring in DC motor:
choices: Slip rings maintain continuous connection → AC output. Split-ring reverses connections → DC output
Slip rings are for DC; commutators for AC
questions.explanation: Slip rings don't reverse connections → current alternates naturally (AC). Commutator reverses every half-turn → current always flows one way (DC).

questions.stem: Which material would NOT be attracted to a magnet?
choices: Aluminium can — not a magnetic material
questions.explanation: Only iron, cobalt, nickel (and their alloys) are magnetic. Aluminium, copper, gold, silver, and most other metals are non-magnetic.
